## Results

### CCC-RISE framework overview

::: {#fig-1}
![](figures/figure1/figure1.svg){width="6.5in"}

**CCC-RISE deconvolves variation in communication across single cells and conditions.** ({{< panel 1 workflow.1 >}}) RISE projects multi-condition scRNA-seq data into eigen-states and decomposes the resulting aligned condition × eigen-state × gene tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.2 >}}) Communication scores are computed between eigen-states for LR pairs to form a 4D communication tensor.
({{< panel 1 workflow.3 >}}) CPD decomposes the communication tensor into factors describing variation across conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
({{< panel 1 embedding >}}) RISE projections serve as a common embedding basis to visualize cell-to-cell heterogeneity across all conditions.
({{< panel 1 cell-mapping >}}) Sender and receiver eigen-state factors and RISE projections collectively map communication patterns back to single cells.
({{< panel 1 component-interpretation >}}) Each CCC-RISE component represents a communication program defined by the association weights across four dimensions: experimental conditions, sender cells, receiver cells, and LR pairs.
:::

RISE projects cells from multiple conditions onto a shared set of eigen-states, effectively aligning them based on gene expression without requiring *a priori* labeling ({{< fig 1 workflow.1 >}})\ [@doi:10.1016/j.cels.2025.101294].
This alignment step produces a condition × eigen-state × gene tensor that RISE factorizes into components representing patterns of variation across the three modes.
To overcome the limitations of aggregating data into pre-defined cell types, CCC-RISE infers communication directly from RISE's unsupervised eigen-states rather than individual cells or broad populations ({{< fig 1 workflow.2 >}}).
For every experimental condition and ligand--receptor (LR) pair defined in CellChat's interaction database (CellChatDB), a score is calculated for all combinations of sender and receiver eigen-states by taking the product of the sender's ligand expression with the receiver's receptor expression\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
This process yields a four-dimensional tensor of data across experimental conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs.
Finally, to extract patterns from this high-dimensional structure, CCC-RISE employs CPD, which decomposes the tensor into distinct components that each represent a communication program defined by a source of variation across the four modes ({{< fig 1 workflow.3 >}}).

CCC-RISE preserves cell identity through its projection matrices and eigen-state--component associations, which allows for interpretation of CPD factors at single-cell resolution.
The eigen-states define shared gene expression programs, so the projection matrices weight cells from every condition in a common embedding where close proximity reflects transcriptional similarity ({{< fig 1 embedding >}})\ [@arxiv:2012.04456].
Further, by multiplying RISE projections with the sender and receiver eigen-state factors, the associations of individual cells with each communication component are recovered ({{< fig 1 cell-mapping >}}).
CCC-RISE's embeddings and factor matrices thus trace LR signaling programs across conditions without losing the granularity of the underlying single-cell data ({{< fig 1 component-interpretation >}}).

We first applied CCC-RISE to a dataset in which conditions represented individual bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples from lung transplant patients with and without acute lung allograft dysfunction (ALAD) ({{< fig alad-cohort cohort >}})\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2024.02.007; @alad-geo].
ALAD is an acute decline in lung function following transplantation that either resolves or progresses to chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD), a predominantly irreversible loss of graft function that leads to re-transplantation or death\ [@doi:10.1016/j.trre.2021.100626; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2026.01.006; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2019.03.009].
Each sample was defined by status at the time of collection (control/no ALAD, ALAD-recovered, and ALAD-declined) and by status six months after collection (stable, ALAD-recovered, declined to CLAD, or died) ({{< tbl alad-outcome-groups >}}).
We used this cohort to establish how a CCC-RISE model is selected, validated, and interpreted.

We selected the RISE rank by bi-cross-validation (BiCV), which fits RISE to a random half of all cells and genes and scores the fit's ability to predict the held-out block of cells and genes\ [@doi:10.1214/08-AOAS227].
Held-out R^2^X rose steeply, plateaued around rank 10, and reached a maximum at rank 17, which we used to construct the communication tensor ({{< fig 2 rise-rank-selection >}}).
Seeking a similarly definitive rank selection criterion for CPD, we evaluated the reconstruction and imputation accuracy (i.e., the accuracy with which the outer product of CPD factors approximates either the original communication tensor or entries held out during fitting, respectively) of CPD models at varying ranks.
Both CPD fit R^2^X and imputation R^2^X generally increased with rank, indicating that higher-rank CPD models did not lose predictive accuracy ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.1 >}}).
However, neither metric provided a specific choice for CPD rank, so we turned from prediction accuracy to between-component collinearity (a measure of degeneracy) and fit-to-fit instability.
Specifically, we varied CPD rank and initialization seed, refit CPD to the communication tensor, compared components within fits by cosine similarity, and compared converged optima across fits by factor match score (FMS).
The cross-component collinearity within condition, sender eigen-state, and receiver eigen-state modes increased rapidly with rank, a trend that was stable across starts ({{< fig alad-cohort cp-collinearity >}}).
Conversely, the LR pair mode became collinear in at least one start at rank 8 ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.2 >}}).
Shared patterns in smaller modes were expected because of the limited number of variation sources among conditions and eigen-states, whereas collinearity in the largest mode (LR pairs) indicated loss of identifiability; it became non-trivial to separate shared communication patterns from artifacts of overfitting at high rank\ [@{doi:10.1002/1099-128X(200005/06)14:3<229::AID-CEM587>3.0.CO;2-N}].
Further, re-initialized factorizations became unstable at rank 7 and beyond, which, combined with the emergence of collinearity at rank 8, encouraged us to decompose the communication tensor at CPD rank 6 ({{< fig 2 cp-rank-selection.3 >}}).
Applied to the ALAD cohort, these rank selection techniques yielded a CCC-RISE model that described 17 gene expression patterns across conditions and eigen-states through RISE and 6 communication programs across conditions, sender eigen-states, receiver eigen-states, and LR pairs through CPD ({{< fig alad-cohort factors genes >}}; {{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices >}}).

We next asked whether the communication programs captured by CCC-RISE were stable, robust against cell permutation, and aligned with external biological validation.
At the selected rank, RISE and CPD factors were stable over re-initialization and leave-one-patient-out jackknife ({{< fig 2 aggregate-fms >}}).
Two components (RISE 3 and CPD 4) were especially sensitive to withheld patients, likely due to their dependence on a small subset of heavily weighted samples ({{< fig alad-cohort rise-fms cpd-fms >}}; {{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.1 >}}; {{< fig alad-cohort factors >}}).
Next, to assess robustness, we extended the significance testing of CellPhoneDB and CellChat to continuous eigen-states by shuffling which cell's expression is paired with each eigen-state projection and recomputing the communication tensor\ [@doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x; @doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
While only 10% of each LR pair's entries exceeded this null at p < 0.05, mean observed scores exceeded mean null scores for nearly every LR pair, indicating that aggregate LR scores, driven by select individual communication tensor entries, were robust to cell permutation ({{< fig alad-cohort permutation-fraction >}}; {{< fig 2 permutation-lr-significance >}}).
Finally, we tested whether each component's receiver cells showed transcriptional evidence of ligand signaling by scoring how well differential expression in the component's top receiver cells recovered each ligand's NicheNet-predicted downstream gene targets\ [@doi:10.1038/s41592-019-0667-5; @doi:10.1038/s41596-024-01121-9].
Weighting each ligand by its loading in the component, mean target scores exceeded those obtained with the shuffled receiver labels for components 2 and 6 ({{< fig 2 nichenet >}}).
Thus, the receiver cells of components 2 and 6 upregulated the downstream gene targets of the ligands most heavily weighted by those components.
Other components were trending toward significance but likely remained underpowered due to the limited overlap between the NicheNet v2 database and CellChatDB (e.g., component 5, q = 0.054, missing GZMA and CD69).
Collectively, these results show that CCC-RISE components were stable, robust to cell permutations, and aligned with external NicheNet ligand--target predictions.

RISE eigen-states allow cellular identity to be traced from CPD component weights back to single-cell gene expression without depending on prior annotations.
We illustrate this with component 6, whose sender and receiver loadings were spread across multiple eigen-states, suggesting signaling between populations ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.2 cp-factor-matrices.3 >}}; {{< fig cmp5-identity cmp-eigenstate-loadings >}}).
Combining these loadings with each cell's RISE projections gave per-cell sender and receiver weights, which few cells carried simultaneously; thresholding defined 67 sender and 58 receiver cells with weights at least 0.3 times the top cell's sender or receiver weight, respectively ({{< fig 2 sender-receiver-strata >}}).
We found that these groups both expressed canonical epithelial marker genes (FXYD3, EPCAM, and ELF3) at higher levels than all other cells ({{< fig cmp5-identity celltype-markers >}}).
Individually, the groups expressed unique epithelial subpopulation markers, indicating communication between ciliated sender cells and basal/secretory receiver cells ({{< fig 2 epithelial-markers >}}; {{< fig cmp5-identity sender-vs-receiver >}}).
Further, all subpopulation markers remained significantly differentially expressed between sender and receiver groups across threshold definitions ({{< fig cmp5-identity sender-vs-receiver tau-sweep >}}).
These eigen-state--derived epithelial labels aligned closely with available annotations but represented non-overlapping subpopulations more granular than those defined in the data ({{< fig 2 celltype-composition >}}).
In sum, label-free interpretation of CCC-RISE factors isolated a well-validated CCC program, wherein ciliated epithelial cells secrete betacellulin (BTC) that binds basal and secretory epithelial cells through epidermal growth factor receptors EGFR and ERBB2, inducing tissue repair or fibrosis depending on disease context ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.4 >}})\ [@doi:10.1165/ajrcmb.20.5.3308; @doi:10.3390/cells11060986].

Having demonstrated CCC-RISE's capacity to resolve cellular subpopulation heterogeneity, we next asked whether CCC-RISE components were associated with clinical outcome.
The proportional abundances of the coarse cell types in these samples showed no significant difference between control, recovered, and declined samples, confirming that cell-type composition did not trivially drive patient associations ({{< fig alad-associations celltype-proportions >}}).
ANOVA of each component's condition loadings against patient outcomes revealed significant associations between CPD component 5 and three outcomes after multiple-test correction: six-month outcome---comprising stable, ALAD-recovered, CLAD, and died groups---and six-month and one-year death ({{< fig 3 outcome-association >}}; {{< fig alad-associations cp-associations >}}).
The lack of association with ALAD status likely reflects the clinical heterogeneity of ALAD diagnosis, which relies on acute, potentially transient reductions in forced expiratory volume (FEV~1~), whereas CLAD and mortality represent more consistently defined endpoints\ [@doi:10.1016/j.healun.2026.01.006; @doi:10.1016/j.healun.2019.03.009].
The same test applied to the condition loadings of RISE components yielded no significant associations, suggesting that outcome associations emerged only through inferred intercellular communication ({{< fig alad-associations rise-associations >}}).

Component 5's sender and receiver factors were both loaded almost exclusively by eigen-state 16, onto which the lymphocyte cluster of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, and natural killer (NK) cells projected most strongly ({{< fig 2 cp-factor-matrices.2 cp-factor-matrices.3 >}}; {{< fig 3 celltype-eigenstates >}}).
However, the lymphocyte cluster was non-uniformly loaded onto eigen-state 16, suggesting that CPD component 5 represented communication among a subset of lymphocytes ({{< fig 3 celltype-pacmap >}}).
Per-cell sender and receiver weights on component 5 were nearly identical, indicating that the same cells were acting as both senders and receivers of component 5 signals ({{< fig 3 sender-receiver-scatter >}}).
Component 5's top LR pairs consisted of markers of immune cell activation (GZMA--F2R), markers of inhibition/exhaustion (CLEC2D--KLRB1 and NECTIN3--TIGIT), mediators of immune-synapse formation (CD70--CD27, CD69--KLRB1, and CD48--CD244), and immune-activating chemokines and their receptors (CCL4/CCL5--CCR4/CCR5 and CXCL13--CXCR3) ({{< fig 3 lr-loadings >}}).
CPD component 5 thus collectively represented an inflammatory communication axis within activated immune populations that was upregulated in CLAD-positive and deceased lung transplant recipients.

CPD groups LR pairs based on co-variation across conditions, senders, and receivers rather than by their association with outcome.
Indeed, while some of component 5's top LR pairs exhibited strong individual association with outcome, they were not the only highly associated LR pairs and were not defined as a group by their ability to stratify patients ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.1 >}}).
Individual outcome association therefore did not explain which LR pairs component 5 grouped together.
Instead, component 5's top LR pairs were more strongly correlated with one another across conditions than randomly drawn LR pairs, LR pairs with similar mean expression to top pairs (i.e., the 20 closest pairs in log mean score), or other LR pairs associated with six-month outcome ({{< fig 3 coordinated-changes.2 >}}).
The expression-matched and outcome-associated baselines confirmed that neither shared abundance nor shared clinical associations were the source of this coordination.
Thus, by modeling variation across conditions, cells, and LR pairs, CCC-RISE isolated coordinated communication axes from sets of individually varying programs.

Given the limited size of the ALAD cohort and the small number of patients in the "died" group, we tested whether the component 5 association could be explained by patient covariates, individual patients, or random patient grouping.
No patient covariate (besides Caucasian ethnicity, which was weakly associated with one-year death) was associated with outcome, even before multiple-test correction ({{< fig alad-associations covariates >}}).
Further, the six-month outcome association remained significant in 40 of 45 leave-one-patient-out jackknife replicates ({{< fig alad-associations effect-size-distributions significant-fraction >}}).
In one of the five exceptions, the held-out patient had died and carried the highest component 5 loading; in the other four, the held-out patients were controls or ALAD-recovered with ordinary condition loadings.
While the association remained significant for most held-out patients, the five failures point to the low statistical power of the ALAD data.
Still, the coordinated communication program represented by the associated component is a real biological pattern present in the expression data.
We next applied scDiffCom's condition-label permutation scheme to our communication tensor by testing whether each LR pair's difference in communication score between CLAD/died and stable/recovered samples exceeded those obtained with permuted patient outcome labels\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x].
Five of the top 10 LR pairs in component 5 had significantly higher communication scores in CLAD/died samples, indicating that scores constructed through RISE exceeded chance in their ability to stratify patients, but only a subset of LR pairs drove the overall association ({{< fig 3 lr-permutation lr-volcano >}}).

The choice of CCC scoring method used in constructing the communication tensor is a known source of disagreement between inference tools, so we asked whether the programs described by components 5 and 6 were dependent on our choice of expression-product scoring\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-30755-0; @doi:10.1038/s41576-020-00292-x].
We compared four approaches used to convert expression to LR interaction scores: product, used by CCC-RISE and NATMI\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-020-18873-z]; mean, used by Tensor-cell2cell and CellPhoneDB\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1038/s41596-020-0292-x]; geometric mean (gmean), used by scDiffCom\ [@doi:10.1038/s43587-023-00514-x]; and the Hill-function-inspired score used by CellChat\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-021-21246-9].
Upon recomputing the communication tensor from a single RISE fit using each scoring method, we observed that each alternate score generally yielded a CPD fit closely matching that of the product score ({{< fig ccc-scoring factor-match >}}).
The alternate scores captured LR pairs similar to those of the product score, especially in components 5 and 6 ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.1 >}}).
Similarly, every score implicated the same coarse sender and receiver cell types in components 5 and 6 except the mean and gmean scores, which pointed to epithelial cells as receivers of component 5's immune signals ({{< fig ccc-scoring interpretation.2 >}}).
Overall, CCC-RISE's expression-product score generally agreed with other available scoring methods, and most disagreements were confined to one or two methods in a single mode of a single component.

We next sought to extend CCC-RISE to an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) dataset (IBDverse), representing a biologically distinct disease context with enhanced statistical power compared with the ALAD dataset\ [@doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02634-7; @ibdverse-arrayexpress].
In the IBD data, conditions comprised terminal-ileum pinch biopsies from individual donors in three groups: healthy, CD uninflamed, and CD inflamed, where CD denotes Crohn's disease ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection cohort >}}).
We selected the IBD ranks with the same BiCV and CPD analyses as for ALAD to construct a CCC-RISE model on IBDverse.
Unlike for ALAD, held-out R^2^X in the RISE BiCV sweep plateaued with no clear maximum, so we used rank 60, the smallest rank within one standard error of the largest held-out R^2^X (rank 85), to decompose the normalized expression tensor ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection rise-rank-selection bicv-test >}}).
Again, CPD fit R^2^X did not provide a clear choice of rank, but the collinearity criteria did: the LR pair mode first became collinear at rank 7, so we decomposed the communication tensor at rank 6 ({{< fig ibd-rank-selection cp-r2x-starts mode-collinearity >}}).
CCC-RISE yielded components that described healthy and inflamed gut communication programs, including opposing activating/inhibitory immune signaling (components 1 and 5), myeloid-driven axon maintenance (component 2), and hormone secretion (components 3--4) ({{< fig 4 cp-factor-matrices >}}; {{< fig ibd-rank-selection factors eigenstate-heatmap >}}).

The data describe several diverse communication programs, so we tested the associations of CPD condition loadings with biopsy type to narrow our interpretation to clinically relevant programs.
While many components tracked three-way inflammation status and distinguished healthy from CD samples, only components 3 and 4 were able to differentiate CD sample inflammation states ({{< fig ibd-associations cp-associations >}}).
Unlike ALAD associations, IBD component 3 and 4 condition loadings were higher in uninflamed than inflamed CD samples, indicating a loss of communication following inflammation ({{< fig ibd-associations status-loadings >}}).
Cell-type compositions directly tracked condition state: immune cells increased, and epithelial cells decreased in abundance with inflammation ({{< fig ibd-associations lineage-proportions covariates >}}).
Thus, CPD components were associated with inflammation status and tracked cell-type composition, as expected for a disease characterized by immune cell invasion and epithelial cell death\ [@doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2023.01.002].

CPD components 3 and 4 represented distinct but complementary hormone-signaling axes.
They were associated with similar sender eigen-states---albeit with distinct distributions---that collectively defined a subpopulation of enteroendocrine (EE) cells.
Conversely, their receiver eigen-states were entirely distinct and uniquely associated with either enterochromaffin (EC) cells (component 3) or tuft cells (component 4) ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes eigenstate-loadings eigenstate-composition >}}).
We therefore restricted our analysis to EE, EC, and tuft cells (as annotated in the data) and visualized single-cell heterogeneity in the component 3/4 signaling axis using RISE projection embeddings ({{< fig 4 ee-state-map.1 >}}; {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes cell-map type-map >}}).
Cells with high sender weights in components 3 and 4 inhabited distinct regions of the broader EE cell cluster, but partially overlapped with each other, suggesting that the components represented a non-exclusive pair of EE subpopulations ({{< fig 4 ee-state-map.2 ee-state-map.3 >}}).
Further, cells with the highest expression of PYY predominantly overlapped with those of high component 3 sender weight, and those with high GCG (GLP-1) expression overlapped with those of high component 4 sender weight, indicating that sender groups were primarily defined by the gene expression of those two hormones ({{< fig 4 hormone-expression-map >}}).
Component 3 and 4 receiver cells were trivially non-overlapping and also matched the expression levels of their respective receptors (NPY1R and GLP1R) ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes receiver-map-c3 receptor-maps.2 >}}).

We went on to characterize the overlapping EE subpopulations represented by components 3 and 4.
There was no clear separation of cells by component 3/4 per-cell sender weight, which pointed to the hormonal plasticity of EE cells within the GLP-1-producing lineage ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-scatter >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.12.029].
Transforming the sender weight axes to polar coordinates and measuring the distribution of cells over polar angles revealed that two states dominated the continuum of cell identities ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}; {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes magnitude-hist >}}).
Acknowledging the continuous nature of these populations, we grouped the cells by polar coordinate into component 3-high, mixed, and component 4-high groups and compared the groups' expression of canonical markers ({{< fig 4 hormone-angle-hist >}}).
The groups of cells were characterized by distinct gene expression: component 3-high cells expressed hormones associated with villus EE cells, component 4-high cells expressed crypt-associated genes, and mixed cells expressed CCK, which marks the intermediate stage between GLP-1-producing and villus cells ({{< fig 4 hormone-extreme-markers >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.036; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.12.029; @doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02634-7].
Further, the crypt-to-villus transition is driven by BMP activity, and we saw a stepwise increase in expression of BMP targets from crypt-like to mixed to villus-like cells ({{< fig 4 hormone-extreme-markers >}})\ [@doi:10.1038/s41556-018-0143-y; @doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.04.036].
All genes except the intermediate marker CCK remained differentially expressed between crypt- and villus-like cells across magnitude thresholds up to 0.9, after which low cell counts reduced statistical power ({{< fig ibd-hormone-axes marker-floor-sweep >}}).
In agreement with the loss of function following inflammation indicated by component 3 associations, component 3-high cells contributed less to the overall EE population in a stepwise manner over healthy, CD uninflamed, and CD inflamed biopsies, indicating that more-exposed, villus-like cells are more sensitive to inflammatory pressure compared with other EE subpopulations ({{< fig ibd-associations status-loadings.1 >}}; {{< fig ibd-hormone-axes extreme-share >}}).
In sum, CCC-RISE components 3 and 4 described sender cells on a continuum between two prevailing states with distinct activity: crypt-like producers of GCG communicating with tuft cells and villus-like producers of PYY communicating with EC cells.

To identify CCC patterns revealed only through single-cell resolution, we compared CCC-RISE with three multi-condition pseudobulk methods.
Tensor-cell2cell and STACCato served as external benchmarks, each with its own communication score, decomposition, and rank selection\ [@doi:10.1038/s41467-022-31369-2; @doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2026.05.005].
Pseudobulk CPD served as a matched ablation to CCC-RISE by replacing the RISE-derived communication tensor with a pseudobulked version.
To test sensitivity to annotation granularity, we fit each comparator method to both cohorts using each cohort's provided coarse and fine cell-type labels ({{< fig comparator-rank-selection pb-fit-coarse stac-shares-fine >}}; {{< tbl cohort-cell-types >}}).
The published Tensor-cell2cell analysis keeps only cell types present in every condition, so to avoid omitting substantial data, we kept every cell type and left out of the fit any communication score whose sender or receiver cell type was absent from that condition.
The other two comparators instead set missing communication scores to zero.

We first evaluated whether the comparators recovered each CCC-RISE component's LR pairs.
Each comparator fit grouped LR pairs through the columns of its LR pair factor, hereafter called LR columns.
For each CCC-RISE component, we identified the closest LR column across all comparator fits by squared cosine similarity between LR pair loadings ({{< fig 5 cos2-grid >}}; {{< fig comparator-split ibd-best >}}).
Components with one or two top LR pairs closely matched single comparator columns, but matches dropped sharply for components as they broadened to three or more top LR pairs ({{< fig 5 cos2-pairs >}}).
Because a comparator could distribute a component's LR pairs across several LR columns, we also computed the fraction of each component's LR pair loadings reconstructed by the best combination of LR columns in each comparator fit ({{< fig 5 span-containment >}}; {{< fig comparator-split ibd-containment >}}).
Only STACCato's fine fit reconstructed broad components by combining columns, accounting for most of ALAD component 3 and IBD component 1 even though its closest single column matched less than half of either component.
Both pseudobulk CPD fits, in contrast, reconstructed little more of any component than its closest column.
Tensor-cell2cell essentially matched no CCC-RISE component and instead tracked the number of genes detected per cell in each condition, so we omitted it from the remaining comparisons ({{< fig comparator-split depth >}}).
Broad CCC-RISE programs associated with many LR pairs therefore had no single counterpart in any comparator, and no comparator fit reconstructed every component.

We next characterized what biological information comparators failed to represent when they divided a CCC-RISE component's top LR pairs among several LR columns.
ALAD component 5 represented a broad program of 11 top LR pairs (i.e., those carrying 90% of its squared loading) and was associated with patient outcomes ({{< fig 5 pair-columns >}}).
STACCato partly reconstructed this program across coarse and fine fits, whereas pseudobulk CPD reconstructed none of it ({{< fig 5 span-containment >}}).
Even so, STACCato's best combination of columns weighted mainly the KLRB1 pairs and CD70--CD27, leaving out the chemokine, cytotoxicity, and immune checkpoint pairs ({{< fig 5 pair-columns >}}).
Moreover, none of the STACCato columns holding these pieces co-varied beyond expression-matched pairs or were associated with patient outcomes ({{< fig comparator-split alad-covariation >}}; {{< fig 5 labels-alad >}}).
Only by grouping the KLRB1 and CD70--CD27 pairs with the other immune LR pairs did CCC-RISE reveal their co-variation and tie the LR pairs to patient outcomes.
Further, across ALAD, three of the five testable CCC-RISE components co-varied, whereas none of the testable comparator columns did, regardless of how many top LR pairs they carried.
CCC-RISE therefore revealed coordinated signaling programs by grouping LR pairs that varied together across samples, whereas comparators split these programs into columns that did not resolve their coordination.

In the reverse direction, we investigated which outcome-associated programs comparators identified that CCC-RISE did not, and whether those programs persisted across cell-type granularity.
Of the 11 outcome-associated comparator LR columns, five placed less than half of their squared loading on the top LR pairs of any CCC-RISE component ({{< fig comparator-missed alad-share ibd-share >}}; {{< fig 5 labels-alad labels-ibd >}}).
These five columns reduced to three signaling programs, two in ALAD carrying AREG--EGFR and TNFSF11--TNFRSF11A/B and one in IBD joining CXCR1/CXCR2 ligands with SAA1--FPR2 ({{< fig comparator-missed alad-contents ibd-contents >}}).
The IBD program, which IBD component 5 partly covered through other CXCR1/CXCR2 ligands, appeared in both comparators and both STACCato fits, whereas each ALAD program appeared in only a single column at a single granularity.
More broadly, 11 of the 30 coarse comparator columns lacked a counterpart in the same method's fine fit, and only two of the seven outcome-associated coarse columns had an outcome-associated fine counterpart.
By contrast, when we refit CCC-RISE at a lower RISE rank, every lower-rank component, except one that loaded almost entirely on NEGR1--NEGR1, had a higher-rank counterpart, and all three outcome-associated components remained outcome-associated at both ranks.
Thus, CCC-RISE partly missed the IBD CXCR1/CXCR2 program, but most comparator associations changed with cell-type label granularity, whereas raising the RISE rank preserved low-rank components and their associations while adding new ones.

Finally, when a comparator LR column matched a CCC-RISE component's LR pairs, we compared how each method assigned the communicating sender and receiver cells.
Because pseudobulk comparators score communication between cell types, matched columns assigned signaling to whole cell types, whereas CCC-RISE components localized it to subpopulations within annotated types ({{< fig 5 flow-alad flow-ibd >}}).
In ALAD, STACCato's fine fit placed BTC--EGFR signaling from epithelial cells to themselves, whereas component 6 sent it from ciliated to basal/secretory epithelial cells.
In IBD, STACCato's fine fit sent PYY--NPY1R and GCG--GLP1R from all EE cells to all EC and tuft cells, respectively, whereas components 3 and 4 drew PYY from villus-like and GCG from crypt-like EE cells along a continuum.
Because CCC-RISE weights cells by eigen-state rather than directly by ligand and receptor expression, we assessed whether a direct expression-based single-cell measure also supported these subpopulations.
For this task, we used NICHES rather than Scriabin, whose interaction programs were inconsistent between random seeds ({{< fig comparator-single-cell scriabin-seeds >}})\ [@doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btac775; @doi:10.1038/s41587-023-01782-z].
NICHES scores each cell's ligand or receptor expression weighted by the condition's mean expression of the matching partner, and we called a cell NICHES-positive when this score was non-zero for any of a component's top ligands or receptors.
Indeed, every CCC-RISE sender and receiver population contained a larger fraction of NICHES-positive cells than predicted from the NICHES-positive rates of its cells' own fine cell types within each sample ({{< fig 5 niches-fraction >}}).
This trend held across most per-cell weight thresholds used to define CCC-RISE sender and receiver populations ({{< fig comparator-single-cell alad-weights ibd-tau >}}).
Hence, although CCC-RISE does not score communication directly from expression, its subpopulations were enriched for cells expressing their components' ligands and receptors relative to their nearest fine cell types.
